index.meta.title: Rumi in South African languages
index.meta.subtitle: What we measured in isiZulu, isiXhosa and Sesotho, with Sepedi, Afrikaans and Setswana also tested.
index.meta.dateline: Measured 7 October 2026 · every number is labelled measured, AI-judged or native ear pending

index.answer.heading: The answer
index.answer.lead: Yes, with three conditions. On automated tests Rumi reads the curriculum, plans and voices lessons, transcribes speech and drafts coaching in isiZulu, isiXhosa and Sesotho. No native speaker has checked a word yet.
bullets: Lesson plans and coaching are strong in all three languages; listening is the capability that separates them.
Six languages, four capabilities, about eighty dollars of metered model and voice calls.
index.answer.table_note: Scores are out of 10 and never round up. Click any cell to go to its evidence.

index.method.heading: How we tested
index.method.lead: Two pipelines, six languages, English as the control; every score compares Rumi's output with a known-good reference by script.
bullets: Curriculum page to lesson plan: a vision model reads the official CAPS pages and the Department's Grade 1 workbook [[fn:fn-caps-zu]] [[fn:fn-wb-zu]]; a planner cuts Term 1 into fifty traceable days; a writer drafts and voices each lesson in the structured format partners use [[fn:fn-rti]].

Classroom recording to coaching report: the best transcription engine writes the transcript; the coaching engine reads it against the partners' coaching course [[fn:fn-coaching-course]], quotes a timed moment for every step it credits, and drafts the debrief.

References: the official file's own text, human transcripts of read speech [[fn:fn-fleurs]] [[fn:fn-nchlt]], the lesson transcript, and the spoken script. The three labels are explained below the diagrams.
index.method.samples: Feasibility-sized samples, not a benchmark: 19 lesson plans and 6 two-week overviews; 143 curriculum, workbook and reader pages; 32 to 70 read sentences per language; 12 classroom recordings (3 partner, 9 public); 6 spoken sentences per voice.
index.method.limits: Listening scores come from read speech in quiet rooms, an upper bound for a Grade 1 classroom. The World Bank structure check [[fn:fn-wb-tool]] tests structure our template enforces, so it sits beside the lesson-plan score, not in it.

index.also_tested.heading: Also tested
index.also_tested.lead: Sepedi, Afrikaans and Setswana ran the same tests without a page of their own; coaching was not run for Afrikaans and Setswana (no classroom recording sourced).

lines.nso: Sepedi (Funda Wande's Limpopo language; not Sesotho): coaching was run on one public reading lesson [[fn:fn-video-nso]]. The transcription engines disagree most here (19.0% to 36.6% of classroom characters on two public lessons [[fn:fn-video-nso-2]], AI-judged), so the agreement gate matters most.
lines.af: Afrikaans: the strongest listening of the six, and the only language with a first-language voice available.
lines.tn: Setswana: the winning engine is fragile on longer audio, so the runner-up is the safer choice; the voice is intelligibility-uncertain until a native ear decides.

index.also_tested.note: Sesotho and Setswana listening is scored on short read phone prompts with their own South African English control [[fn:fn-nchlt]], not the sentence set used for the other four [[fn:fn-fleurs]]; the two are not comparable.

index.scheme.heading: Scheme of studies for one book
index.scheme.lead: One Department of Basic Education workbook, turned into a week-by-week scheme that traces every lesson to its curriculum requirement; the sheet is open to anyone.
bullets: The six CAPS Home Language editions are one document in six languages (same sections, same Term 1 tables, same time tables); one configuration per language turned all six into requirement lists.
Book 1: 142 pages, 64 worksheets, four a week, eight workbook weeks a term; CAPS has ten, so weeks 9 and 10 carry no workbook pages. Arithmetic slips in the official PDFs are flagged, not inherited.
The workbook's order of new sounds differs from our CAPS-first plan (isiZulu workbook a, i, e, o, m, u…; our days a, e, i, o, u, m…); the sheet shows both, so the gap is visible.

index.ship.heading: What it would take to ship
index.ship.lead: The infrastructure work is small and known; the expensive part is one first-language reviewer per language for about an hour.
rows: Use the engine that scored best for each language for transcription, with a two-engine agreement gate so a transcription slip can never become a coaching question
Review the flagged lesson phrases (about seventy across six languages), one transcript and one voice note
one Foundation Phase teacher or coach per language, about an hour
Record one consented three-minute clip per language, so Rumi speaks in a South African coach's own voice
Share classroom recordings, lesson plans and the coaching course's field observation tool
Keep the back-translation check in the lesson pipeline; it caught errors the structure checklist cannot see
Make every pilot teacher a rater: one sentence of Rumi's voice, then a tick, a cross or a "say it right" reply

index.partners.heading: What the partners can give us
index.partners.lead: Four things, in order of how much each moves the numbers.
bullets: Native-speaker ratings: an hour each from a teacher or coach in each of the six languages.
A coach's voice: one consented three-minute recording per language.
Classroom recordings and structured lesson plans in isiXhosa, Sesotho and Sepedi; one Afrikaans recording completes the table.
The coaching course as used in the field: its observation tool, the teacher reflection instrument, and term plans or pacing guides per grade.

index.cost.heading: What this cost
index.cost.lead: About eighty dollars of metered model and voice calls for six languages, four capabilities, 19 lesson plans, 12 classroom recordings and about 300 speech tests; authoring and judging ran on subscription seats.

lesson_plans.heading: Lesson plans
lesson_plans.lead: Score 9.2: Rumi reads the official pages faithfully, cuts Term 1 into traceable days and writes real isiZulu.
bullets: Page misses are printer stamps and tracing rows, not words; five curriculum items are taught but paraphrased.
The only language below the real-word cap: the unattested words (namuhla, ikhanda, amahlombe) are everyday words the sources never use.
Fourteen uncertain phrases await a first-language coach.
lesson_plans.note: Beside the score: World Bank structure check 9.7 (AI-judged, two graders, three lessons) [[fn:fn-wb-tool]]. Only back-translation found "first bear" where "first sound" was meant.

listening.heading: Listening
listening.names_note: Names in the video become [learner], [teacher] and [school]. Remarks to camera are labelled "Teacher (interview)" and are not coached.
listening.score_line: Gemini 2.5 Pro on 32 read sentences with human transcripts: 5.8% of characters wrong; English from the same set 1.6%.
listening.agreement_line: On this video the two best engines disagree on 16.4% of characters. No human transcript exists for classroom audio, so this is a proxy, not an accuracy score.
listening.lead: Score 8.8: the best engine gets 5.8% of characters wrong on read isiZulu.
bullets: The runner-up is under two points behind; a second set of short phone prompts agrees [[fn:fn-nchlt]]. On this video the engines disagree mostly on names, chants and songs.
A two-engine agreement gate stops a misheard name becoming a coaching question, as once happened in an earlier run.

coaching.heading: Coaching
coaching.not_graded: The teacher is never graded: steps seen, partly seen or not observed, each with a timed quote, and one next step.
coaching.accuracy_note: These measure Rumi, not the teacher: quotes found, items filled, agreement across three runs.
coaching.lead: Score 9.6 comes from three partner training videos, analysed privately [[fn:fn-vvob-videos]]: 97.2% of quotes found, 93.3% of steps addressed, three runs in close agreement. Below, a full report on the public lesson above.
bullets: The instrument discriminates: a staged demonstration and a real lesson of the same strand came out clearly apart; the stricter reader used below named a blockage a more lenient model missed.
AI-judged, beside the score: feedback prose 5.0 out of 10 (understandable, not natural); 21.7% of factual claims flagged unsupported, an over-count including evaluative lines.

speaking.heading: Speaking
speaking.chat_note: The teacher types; Rumi answers in voice notes. Rumi's lines were drafted and checked by two AI models and still need a native ear.
speaking.score_line: ElevenLabs eleven_v4, an English-accented South African voice reading isiZulu: 1.7% of characters lost on the text-to-speech-to-text round trip (6 sentences, measured). Our English voice, on a different ElevenLabs model, lost 0.0%. Native ear pending.
speaking.lead: Score 9.6: no isiZulu voice exists on any engine we can reach, so an English-accented South African voice reads isiZulu.
speaking.note: A second listener loses 11.1%; against human recordings the voice adds 5.8% of error (AI-judged).

ship.heading: What it would take to ship isiZulu
bullets: Use the best-scoring transcription engine with the agreement gate; an hour from a first-language coach (fourteen phrases, one transcript, one voice note) and a three-minute recording for an isiZulu voice.

A twelve-mapping audit of the term plan found ten the same, two partial, none wrong.
Ten flagged phrases (the click's description, the idiom for skipping rope) await a first-language coach.

lesson_plans.heading: Lesson plans
lesson_plans.lead: Score 9.8: near-perfect page reading, every curriculum requirement placed, and vocabulary as attested as a published reader's.
bullets: A twelve-mapping audit found all twelve the same.
Sesotho writes words apart ("Mme o a mema"), which raises the raw real-word rate, so each language is calibrated against its own reader.
Twelve flagged phrases await a first-language coach, led by "O fehla, o fehla" (stirring pap) and "hweshetsa" (whisper).

bullets: The main public sentence set has no Sesotho, so the score uses short phone prompts [[fn:fn-nchlt]] with their own English control; not comparable with isiZulu or isiXhosa.
On this video the engines disagree on a noisy chorus and spelling turns; the other public clip [[fn:fn-video-st-2]] gives 23.9%. One slip reached the coach: n and g heard as "m" and "kh".

coaching.heading: Coaching
coaching.not_graded: The teacher is never graded: steps seen, partly seen or not observed, each with a timed quote, and one next step.
coaching.accuracy_note: These measure Rumi, not the teacher: quotes found, items filled, agreement across three runs.
coaching.lead: Score 9.7: the coaching model found every quote (100.0%), addressed 93.3% of steps, and three runs agreed closely.
bullets: Measured on this public phonics lesson (the sound "ng"; the teacher says Grade 2), instrument mapped from the isiZulu course.
Caution: against the other engine's transcript of the same clip only 25 of 42 quotes are found; on Sesotho classroom audio the transcript itself is the uncertainty.

speaking.score_line: The Soniox voice reading Sesotho: 6.6% of characters lost on the round trip (6 sentences, measured). No English control exists for this engine; our English ElevenLabs voice lost 0.0%. Native ear pending.

speaking.note: A second listener loses 11.5%; against human recordings the voice was recovered better (penalty -10.3%), which says more about the clipped prompts than the voice (AI-judged).

ship.heading: What it would take to ship Sesotho
